Microphone

Low at the bottom, high at the top

Time runs left to right, pitch runs bottom to top, and colour is loudness, from dark blue for quiet to red for loud. Every sound has its own pattern: a voice is a stack of wavy lines, hiss is a haze, and a door slam is a vertical stripe.

A note is a stack of peaks

A piano note isn't one frequency. The lowest peak, the fundamental, is the note you'd name. The evenly spaced peaks above it are harmonics, and their balance is what makes a piano sound like a piano. Isolate a fundamental and it sounds like a plain tone; add its harmonics back and the instrument returns.

Every mic has its own EQ

No mic hears every frequency equally. Its frequency response works like an EQ setting that's baked into everything it records. That's why a lav and a boom on the same actor never quite match, and why dialogue editors EQ one to sit with the other.

A teaching model, not a measurement tool. The mic curves are typical shapes for each type of mic, not measurements of a particular model. Isolation uses a 4096-point FFT filter, about 12 Hz per step at 48 kHz, so low notes that sit close together can't be separated as cleanly as high ones. Recordings are mixed to mono, and only the first 60 seconds of your own recordings are used.
